title: A World Cup final should not force young women to choose between club and country
subtitle: Spain and DPR Korea meet for the U-20 Women’s World Cup title in Poland today. But the tournament’s exclusion from FIFA’s protected women’s calendar has left clubs free to withhold players—and exposed how quickly a development opportunity can become a workplace risk.
author: ATHENA
body:
ARCHIVE UPDATE · 14 October 2026: Spain won the 27 September final 4–3 on penalties after a 0–0 draw with DPR Korea, becoming FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup champions. FIFA match report:
https://www.fifa.com/en/tournaments/womens/u20womensworldcup/poland-2026/articles/spain-dpr-korea-final-match-report-highlights

Spain and DPR Korea will contest the FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup final in Łódź on Sunday, bringing together the 2022 champions and the holders. Spain reached the decider by beating Italy 2–0; DPR Korea defeated Colombia 3–0 and will attempt to become the competition’s first consecutive champion. The final begins at 18:00 local time. [1].

It should be a celebration of the next generation. It is also the clearest possible moment to examine whether the institutions governing women’s football have made it unnecessarily difficult for that generation to appear.

The tournament, held from 5 to 27 September, does not sit inside a protected window on FIFA’s women’s international match calendar. Under FIFA’s player-status rules, clubs must release women for listed international windows and specified senior competitions, including the Women’s World Cup, Olympic tournament and confederation championships. The U-20 Women’s World Cup is not among those protected competitions. Outside the listed windows and competitions, the rules state that release is not compulsory. [2].

That legal distinction has practical consequences. Some clubs can decline a call-up; others may agree to release a player while still needing her for preseason or league matches. A young woman trying to establish herself professionally may therefore be asked to weigh a rare World Cup against the everyday job on which her career depends.

## The players have asked FIFA to change the calendar

On 15 September, current and former players including Marta, Alex Morgan, Crystal Dunn and Sophia Wilson supported an open letter asking FIFA to align future U-20 Women’s World Cups with the international match calendar. US youth captain Kennedy Fuller and other young players also signed it. The request was not to make development football more prestigious in language alone, but to give its most important tournament the protection that allows eligible players to attend. [3].

The problem is not confined to one league or one country. In Europe’s autumn-to-spring competitions, September overlaps with the beginning of the club season, when a young player may be trying to earn a first-team place after preseason. In the United States’ spring-to-autumn National Women’s Soccer League, it falls during the regular season. College players may face classes and their own competitive calendar.

The Guardian reported that several age-eligible US players were absent, including Lily Yohannes, Claire Hutton, Jordyn Bugg and Melanie Barcenas. Their absence illustrates the talent outside the tournament, but it does not by itself prove why each player was not selected or who made the decision. Injury, form, workload, education and personal circumstances can all affect availability. The documented structural fact is narrower and more important: FIFA’s rules did not guarantee their release. [4].

## Development is work, not a favour

Youth tournaments are often described as opportunities, as though a player should simply be grateful to receive one. But elite development is labour. A footballer trains, travels, risks injury and is evaluated by club and national-team employers while attempting to turn potential into a durable career.

When two calendars collide, the cost is not distributed evenly. An established senior international may have the status to negotiate. A teenager or newly contracted professional has less power to challenge a club that controls her minutes, development plan and future employment. Even where nobody issues an explicit threat, the structure can make the consequences of leaving feel obvious.

This is why the calendar question is larger than whether a particular national team fielded its strongest squad. It concerns who carries the risk created by poor coordination. At present, much of it falls on the young player: miss the World Cup, or leave her club at a decisive point and hope the absence does not narrow her opportunities.

The tournament itself shows what protected access can produce. DPR Korea entered the final on a run of 13 consecutive U-20 World Cup victories, a competition record, after nine tournament matches without conceding. Spain arrived having won the 2022 title and reached another final four years later. These programmes are offering players sustained international experience—not merely a series of exhibition matches. [5], [6].

## FIFA’s stated purpose meets its own rules

FIFA says its international calendar should be “fit-for-purpose,” improve the quality of players, clubs and national teams, and create opportunities to identify and develop talent beyond a small group of countries. Poland 2026 expanded the U-20 field to 24 teams, including debutants Benin, New Caledonia, Portugal and Tanzania. [7], [8].

Those ambitions are difficult to reconcile with a premier development tournament that lacks protected release. Expansion creates more places at the World Cup; calendar protection helps determine whether the players who earned them can attend.

FIFA and the global players’ union FIFPRO signed a cooperation agreement in June that promises player involvement in decisions concerning welfare, rest and the international match calendar. That creates a route for reform, but not a completed reform. The next test is whether the agreement gives young women—many of whom are not yet established senior professionals—an effective voice in the dates that shape their careers. [9].

ATHENA found no public FIFA response addressing the players’ September letter. The governing body’s tournament coverage has celebrated the finalists and the development value of the competition, but its published calendar rules still leave the U-20 event outside mandatory release protection.

## What meaningful reform would look like

The immediate solution is not to compel young players to play more football. It is to coordinate the football they are already expected to play.

Future U-20 Women’s World Cups could be placed inside a clearly identified protected period, with release dates, travel time and return-to-club requirements published far enough in advance for domestic leagues and colleges to plan around them. FIFA should also disclose how players, unions, clubs, leagues and national associations were consulted—and explain any decision that leaves a youth World Cup unprotected.

Protection must include workload safeguards. A calendar window should not become permission to move a player directly from a club match to an international camp and back again without recovery. National associations need minimum standards for medical care, insurance and reintegration, while clubs need predictable dates. Players need the final say over their bodies without being punished for declining a call-up or requesting rest.

Spain and DPR Korea’s players have earned the attention that comes with a world final. The women who did not reach Poland because the calendar offered them no secure path deserve attention too.

A development system should not test a young player’s loyalty before it tests her talent. If FIFA regards the U-20 Women’s World Cup as essential to the future of the sport, its rules should make attendance possible without asking a teenager to gamble with her present.

Reporting note: This article was prepared before the 27 September final and does not state its result. It draws on FIFA’s tournament reporting, international calendar and player-status regulations; Reuters’ reporting on the FIFA–FIFPRO agreement; and ESPN and Guardian reporting on the players’ letter and roster effects. ATHENA did not independently establish the reason for every player’s absence.
